**Copenhagen Fashion Week** (**CPHFW**) is an international biannual fashion event held in **Copenhagen, Denmark**. Established in **2006**, it presents Nordic and international fashion through runway shows, presentations, installations, talks, and related industry events. It is generally held in **January or February** for autumn/winter collections and in **August** for spring/summer collections. **[1]**, **[2]**

{{page:image}}

*Image: Andrea Steen during Copenhagen Fashion Week, **2020**. Wikimedia Commons. Author: **Thomas Razzano**. License: CC BY 2.5. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Andrea_Steen_by_Thomas_Razzano.jpg*

CPHFW has become known for combining the promotion of **Nordic fashion** with mandatory environmental and social admission criteria for brands applying to its official show and presentation schedule. Its **Sustainability Requirements** framework has subsequently been adopted or adapted by other European fashion organizations. **[3]**, **[4]**

## History

The first Copenhagen Fashion Week was held in **2006**, following the consolidation of Danish clothing trade fairs **Dansk Modeuge** and **Dansk Herremodeuge**, whose histories extended back to the **1950s**. The new format brought runway shows, exhibitions, presentations, and commercial fashion activity together under a recurring citywide event. **[2]**, **[5]**

In **2018**, **Cecilie Thorsmark** became chief executive officer. Under the new management, CPHFW established an advisory board of fashion-industry professionals and began developing a more structured environmental and social strategy with the consultancy **In futurum** and other knowledge partners. **[6]**

The organization announced its first Sustainability Action Plan in **2020**. Beginning with the **Autumn/Winter 2023** edition, brands applying for the official show and presentation schedule were required to document compliance with a set of minimum standards. **[3]**, **[7]**

A revised framework was announced in **March 2024** and piloted during subsequent seasons. The updated requirements became the mandatory admission framework for the official schedule, with their full implementation marked during the **Autumn/Winter 2026** edition. **[7]**, **[8]**

In **2026**, Copenhagen Fashion Week celebrated its **20th anniversary** through its Autumn/Winter 2026 and Spring/Summer 2027 editions and a series of international collaborations. **[9]**

## Event Format

Copenhagen Fashion Week is organized around an official schedule of physical showcases and associated cultural and professional programming. The length of individual editions has varied between four and five days.

| Programme element | Description |
|---|---|
| **Runway shows** | Scheduled presentations of seasonal collections |
| **Presentations** | Alternative formats allowing closer viewing of collections |
| **Installations** | Spatial and interdisciplinary fashion projects |
| **Talks** | Discussions about design, business, culture, technology, and environmental or social issues |
| **Events** | Brand activations, exhibitions, receptions, and public or invitation-based programmes |
| **Showrooms** | Spaces where brands present collections to buyers and industry representatives |
| **Trade fair** | The biannual **Copenhagen International Fashion Fair (CIFF)** held alongside fashion week |

The event should be distinguished from **CIFF**, which operates as a separate commercial trade platform at the **Bella Center Copenhagen**. CIFF and the former **Revolver** trade show consolidated their activities in **2023**; current editions operate under the CIFF name. **[10]**, **[11]**

## Organization and Funding

Copenhagen Fashion Week operates as a **non-profit organization**. Its funding model has been described as approximately **15% public funding** and **85% commercial partnerships**, with the **Danish Ministry of Industry, Business and Financial Affairs** identified as its principal public contributor. **[12]**

Commercial partners support the production and international communication of the event. The organization also works with industry associations, consultancies, cultural institutions, brands, media organizations, and public bodies.

## Sustainability Requirements

The **Sustainability Requirements** framework sets admission criteria for brands seeking inclusion in CPHFW’s official show and presentation schedule. The requirements address environmental and social considerations throughout the fashion value chain. **[3]**

The current framework is structured around six focus areas:

| Focus area | Scope |
|---|---|
| **Strategic direction** | Governance, policies, targets, and implementation |
| **Design** | Product development, durability, circularity, and material choices |
| **Smart material choices** | Preferred, certified, recycled, upcycled, and lower-impact materials |
| **Working conditions** | Human rights, due diligence, and conditions within the supply chain |
| **Consumer engagement** | Product information and communication with customers |
| **Showcase production** | Environmental and social considerations in producing shows and presentations |

Earlier versions of the framework required brands to demonstrate that at least **50%** of a collection consisted of certified, preferred, upcycled, recycled, or deadstock materials. The framework has since been revised, and its current structure consists of **19 Minimum Standards** and **87 Additional Actions**. **[3]**, **[7]**

The Minimum Standards are mandatory for admission to the official show and presentation schedule. The Additional Actions are voluntary self-assessment measures intended to help brands map further improvements. Applications and supporting documentation are screened by an external committee led by **Rambøll**. **[3]**

CPHFW states that this procedure is a screening and validation process rather than a formal audit. Compliance therefore does not certify that a brand or its products are “sustainable,” “conscious,” or “eco-friendly”; it indicates only that the applicant has met the event’s admission criteria. **[3]**, **[13]**

## International Adoption

The framework has influenced admission policies beyond Denmark. Organizations associated with **Berlin Fashion Week**, the **British Fashion Council**, and **Amsterdam Fashion Week** have announced programmes based on CPHFW’s Sustainability Requirements. **[4]**, **[14]**, **[15]**

| Organization or event | Announced implementation |
|---|---|
| **Berlin Fashion Week** | Mandatory criteria following an onboarding and pilot period, with full implementation planned for **February 2026** |
| **British Fashion Council** | Integration into the **BFC NEWGEN** programme, with full implementation from **January 2026** |
| **Amsterdam Fashion Week** | Pilot programme followed by planned full implementation in **September 2026** |
| **Norwegian Fashion Hub and Oslo Runway** | Earlier adoption and implementation of the framework |

This expansion has contributed to Copenhagen Fashion Week’s role as a reference point in discussions about environmental and social requirements within international fashion-event production.

## Talent Development

CPHFW also operates **CPHFW NEWTALENT**, a support programme for emerging Nordic designers. Introduced in **2022**, the programme provides selected brands with mentorship, financial support, industry guidance, and access to the official schedule. **[16]**

The initiative works with partner organizations and advisers on subjects including business development, international trade, law, taxation, production, and brand positioning.

## Editions in 2026

The **Autumn/Winter 2026** edition took place from **January 27 to 30, 2026**. It formed part of CPHFW’s 20th-anniversary programme and included shows, presentations, events, and an official talk programme. **[9]**, **[17]**

The **Spring/Summer 2027** edition is scheduled for **August 3–7, 2026**. Its official show and presentation programme includes **34 brands**, alongside talks, exhibitions, installations, and other events. The concurrent CIFF trade fair is scheduled for **August 3–5, 2026**. **[1]**, **[10]**, **[18]**

## Cultural Position

Copenhagen Fashion Week has contributed to the international visibility of Danish and wider Nordic fashion. Its schedules have included established companies, independent labels, emerging designers, and brands from other countries.

The event is frequently positioned outside the traditional four-city fashion calendar of **New York**, **London**, **Milan**, and **Paris**. Its international profile is associated with Scandinavian design, street style, emerging-brand support, and its use of admission requirements as a mechanism for encouraging changes in fashion-industry practice. **[19]**

**Copenhagen Fashion Week NEWTALENT**, also styled **CPHFW NEWTALENT**, is a support programme for emerging Nordic fashion brands established by Copenhagen Fashion Week in 2022. Based around the Copenhagen show calendar, it combines financial assistance, mentoring and opportunities to meet international buyers and press.[1]

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## Origins

The programme was announced on 27 June 2022, with A. Roege Hove, Latimmier and P.L.N. as its first supported brands for the spring/summer 2023 season. Initially supported by Circulose, it brought existing talent-development activities into a formal structure covering business advice, presentation and financial support. Launch collaborators included the Swedish Fashion Council and the graduate-design platform ALPHA.[1]

## Structure

The programme describes its core audience as emerging Nordic brands with fewer than five years in business. It supports three to five designers per season, with each selected brand enrolled for three consecutive seasons. Assistance includes bursaries, mentoring, professional advice, participation in the official show and presentation schedule, and promotion through Copenhagen Fashion Week’s channels.[2]

After the three-season period, brands enter an alumni network that continues to offer business, communication, networking and presentation opportunities. A dedicated showroom introduces participating designers to Nordic and international buyers and journalists.[2]

**One To Watch** is a related recognition category awarded at the discretion of the show and presentation committee. It offers visibility and a presentation or event listing for applicants considered promising but not yet ready for full enrolment; unlike the core programme, it does not include a bursary or mentoring sessions.[2]

## Designers and development

For the SS27 edition, announced in May 2026, Studio Constance joined Stem and Anne Sofie Madsen. Madsen was entering her third and final season, while Stem was returning for its second. Renè, Sson and Taus received One To Watch recognition. The programme was presented by Pandora, with CIFF also supporting it.[3]

The SS27 fashion-week programme, scheduled for 3–7 August 2026, identified Studio Constance as the first Swedish brand to join the core scheme.[4]

Vika Gazinskaya is a Russian fashion designer based in Moscow and the founder of the eponymous label Vika Gazinskaya. Established in 2006, the brand became internationally known for sculptural and exaggerated silhouettes, graphic construction, unusual proportions and a refusal to use natural fur and leather.[1][2][3]

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## Background and early career

Gazinskaya was born in Moscow and studied costume design at the Moscow State University of Service. Early in her career she participated in the Russian Silhouette competition and subsequently presented work at the Smirnoff design competition in Italy.[4]

Before establishing her label, Gazinskaya worked for the Russian edition of *L'Officiel*. Contemporary and retrospective profiles place this period in the early 2000s and describe her work in the magazine's fashion department as an important stage in her development as a designer.[4][5]

In 2006 Gazinskaya founded her own brand in Moscow.[1] Her first collections were presented in Russia before she increasingly began showing and promoting her work internationally.

## Vika Gazinskaya

The Vika Gazinskaya label developed a recognizable visual language based on volume, construction and strong silhouettes. Collections have included oversized coats, shaped shoulders, dresses with deliberately altered proportions, graphic prints and garments whose form is created through cutting rather than extensive surface decoration.[2][6]

Gazinskaya's international visibility grew partly through Paris Fashion Week, where she was photographed wearing pieces from her own collections. The resulting street-style coverage introduced the label to a wider group of international editors and buyers. Gazinskaya later described this attention as an organic development rather than a planned marketing strategy.[7]

By the 2010s, the label was covered regularly by international fashion publications. *Vogue* maintains an archive of Vika Gazinskaya runway collections covering multiple seasons of ready-to-wear.[8]

In 2014 Gazinskaya also created a capsule collection for & Other Stories. The collaboration translated elements associated with her main line — exaggerated proportions, graphic motifs and playful drawing-like prints — into a collection for the international retailer.[9]

## Materials and animal-free fashion

Gazinskaya has consistently avoided natural fur and leather in her collections. In interviews she has connected this position with vegetarianism and concern for animal welfare. Her collections have instead used substitutes including faux leather, faux shearling and wool-based materials.[2][3]

For the Fall 2017 collection, for example, *Vogue* noted the use of faux leather and mock shearling made from machine-treated mohair.[6] In reporting on the Russian luxury market, *Vogue Business* described Gazinskaya as an advocate of animal rights whose label did not use genuine fur or leather.[3]

The designer subsequently expanded these concerns through Vika 2.0, a line associated with recycled and lower-impact materials. In 2021, *Vogue* included a Vika 2.0 dress made from recycled cotton in a selection of environmentally oriented denim designs.[10]

## International recognition

Gazinskaya was a finalist for the ANDAM Fashion Award in 2012.[3] Two years later she became one of the finalists of the inaugural LVMH Prize for Young Fashion Designers. The official LVMH Prize archive identifies her as a Moscow-based Russian designer and records Vika Gazinskaya among the finalists of the 2014 edition.[1][11]

Her clothes have also appeared on actresses and musicians. *Vogue*, for example, documented Kirsten Dunst wearing a Vika Gazinskaya dress at the 2019 Veuve Clicquot Polo Classic in Los Angeles and Bella Heathcote wearing a coat by the designer during the 2020 Sundance Film Festival.[12][13]

## Design identity

Gazinskaya's work is frequently associated with a combination of sculptural construction and playful or deliberately simplified imagery. Her collections can shift between highly structured volumes and softer, draped forms while retaining an emphasis on proportion and silhouette.[6][14]

She has cited fashion history and art as important points of reference while emphasizing the need to transform those references into contemporary forms. In a 2014 interview she described her approach in terms of knowledge of fashion and art history combined with a modern, bold and recognizable aesthetic.[7]

This approach has positioned Vika Gazinskaya within the generation of Moscow-based designers who gained international visibility during the late 2000s and 2010s through a combination of runway presentations, international retail, fashion media and the growing importance of street-style photography.

Tatiana Mamedova (Russian: Татьяна Мамедова) is a Moscow-based fashion designer, artist, costume designer and fashion-show director associated with Russian fashion and film production. Her work has included independent fashion collections, costume design for cinema and the development of uniforms for hospitality projects. Earlier versions of this Indexmod entry also identify her with the labels Ali, EMP.OS and Tatiana Mamedova Atelier.

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## Fashion and performance

Mamedova has worked across fashion design, costume and the staging of fashion presentations. Biographical material published about her states that she trained at the Slava Zaitsev Laboratory of Fashion and later worked in fashion-show production, including Russian Fashion Week. Some secondary sources describe her as the event's chief show director between 2003 and 2006; because detailed archival documentation is limited, this claim is best treated as biographical information rather than a fully independently documented institutional record.[1]

In April 2006 she presented the collection **Sisters of Mercy** (*Сёстры милосердия*) during Fashion Week in Moscow at Art Strelka. Contemporary coverage described the presentation as a combination of fashion, video art and contemporary dance, with clothing ranging from wearable pieces to more sculptural, object-like forms.[2]

The surviving Indexmod chronology also records later projects titled *Symbolism of the Cross* and *Empire of the Sun*, although reliable independent documentation for these projects is limited.

## Film production — Costume designer

Mamedova has worked in film production as a costume designer, developing clothing as part of the visual construction of fictional characters, social groups and environments.

Her best-documented film project is Fyodor Bondarchuk's science-fiction film *The Inhabited Island* (*Обитаемый остров*, 2008), adapted from the novel by Arkady and Boris Strugatsky.[3] Mamedova is credited among the film's costume designers.

The production required an extensive costume system for the fictional planet Saraksh. Published accounts of Mamedova's work describe the development of military uniforms and costumes for different social groups within the film's dystopian society.[1] In this context, costume functioned not only as character clothing but also as part of the film's world-building and visual distinction between institutions, classes and subcultures.

Her work on *The Inhabited Island. Film One* received a nomination for the 2009 Nika Award in the category of **Best Costume Design**.[4][5]

The earlier Indexmod version also listed Fyodor Bondarchuk's *Pritazhenie* as part of her filmography. This credit has not been retained in the confirmed film-production list because reliable production credits supporting Mamedova's participation have not been identified.

## Uniform design

Mamedova has also worked outside runway fashion and cinema. In 2016 she designed uniforms for the staff of the Moscow restaurant **Severyane**. *The Village* described the clothing as visually connected to Russian avant-garde references, while *Afisha Daily* characterized the uniforms as futuristic and associated their geometry with the imagery of Kazimir Malevich.[6][7]

She also created uniforms for other Moscow restaurants associated with restaurateurs Ilya Tyutenkov and William Lamberti, including Uilliam's and Ugolyok.[8]

This part of her practice connects fashion design with applied uniform design, hospitality and interior identity rather than conventional seasonal collections.

## Artistic identity

Mamedova's documented projects repeatedly use themes of futurism, uniform, geometric construction and theatrical presentation. Her fashion shows incorporated performance, while her film costumes developed fictional social and military identities through dress.[1][2]

The 2006 *Sisters of Mercy* presentation, the costumes for *The Inhabited Island* and later hospitality uniforms illustrate a practice positioned between fashion, costume, performance and applied design rather than within a single conventional fashion-label model.

***Updated 2026-09-29***

Artur Lomakin is a Moscow-based Russian fashion designer and photographer, best known as the founder of the independent clothing label **Forget Me Not**. His work combines fashion design and fashion photography and has been discussed in the context of Moscow's independent fashion scene and debates around the so-called post-Soviet aesthetic.[1][2] The earlier Indexmod entry likewise identifies Lomakin as both a designer and photographer and associates him with Forget Me Not.

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## Forget Me Not

Forget Me Not is Lomakin's independent fashion label. By 2015 the brand was established enough for Lomakin to present a photographic series built around its advertising imagery at the Moscow contemporary-art festival DOCA.[1]

DOCA describes Forget Me Not explicitly as Lomakin's clothing brand and identifies him as both a young designer and a fashion photographer. The festival presentation emphasized the relationship between clothing and image-making: rather than presenting garments only as products, Lomakin used photography to construct a visual environment around the label.[1]

The original Indexmod entry dates the founding of Forget Me Not to 2010. Contemporary surviving sources confirm Lomakin as the brand's founder, although easily accessible primary documentation for the precise 2010 founding date is limited.

## Photography

Photography forms a parallel part of Lomakin's practice. At **DOCA-2015** in Moscow he presented a series titled *Forget Me Not*, consisting of photographs from advertising projects for his fashion label.[1]

In the accompanying festival text, Lomakin discussed fashion photography as a field governed by established conventions while arguing that commercial fashion imagery can nevertheless move into the territory of photographic art. He named photographers Willy Vanderperre and Juergen Teller among influences on his photographic approach.[1]

DOCA's later institutional material continued to list Artur Lomakin among photographers who had participated in previous editions of the festival.[3]

## Moscow and the post-Soviet aesthetic

Lomakin became part of international discussion around a generation of designers working in Moscow during the 2010s. In 2017, *1 Granary* included him in a discussion with designer Asiya Bareeva, photographer Turkina Faso and fashion historian Djurdja Bartlett about the meaning and limitations of the term **post-Soviet aesthetic**.[2]

Lomakin described the practical conditions facing independent designers in Moscow in terms of a small domestic market and weak institutional support for emerging fashion. He contrasted independent creative practice with established fashion-week structures and noted the importance of looking beyond Russia for audiences and commercial opportunities.[2]

His participation in this discussion places Forget Me Not within a broader period when international fashion media became increasingly interested in designers, photographers and stylists working with the visual environment of post-Soviet cities. The label should not, however, be reduced to that category alone: Lomakin's documented practice combines clothing, styling and photography rather than operating solely as an interpretation of Soviet or post-Soviet imagery.

## Visual language

Earlier coverage of Lomakin and Forget Me Not associated the label with the peripheral landscapes of Moscow and with an understated, restrained visual vocabulary. The previous Indexmod article described the grey anonymity of Moscow's suburbs as an important reference in his work.

The connection between fashion and location is also visible in Lomakin's photographic work. Clothes, models and urban environments function together as parts of the same image rather than as separate product and background elements.

This approach connects his roles as designer and photographer: Forget Me Not operates not only through individual garments but through the photographs, styling and environments in which the garments are represented.[1]

## Independent fashion

In his comments to *1 Granary*, Lomakin addressed structural difficulties facing independent Russian designers, including limited institutional support, a small market and the difficulty of developing a sustainable fashion business locally.[2]

These comments provide context for Forget Me Not as an independent project. Rather than belonging to one of Russia's established fashion houses, the label emerged within a network of small brands, photographers, stylists and other creative practitioners operating partly outside traditional fashion institutions.

Lomakin's practice consequently sits between commercial fashion, independent publishing imagery and contemporary photography.

***Updated 2026-09-29***

Nina Donis is an independent Russian fashion label founded in Moscow by designers Nina Neretina and Donis Pouppis. Officially launched in 2000, the brand became one of the internationally visible Russian independent fashion projects of the early 2000s, presenting collections in Moscow, London and Milan and developing a visual language based on utilitarian clothing, uniforms, sportswear, modernist construction and references to Russian and Soviet culture.[1][2][3]

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## Founders

Nina Neretina and Donis Pouppis met while studying textiles in Moscow in the late 1980s. According to *Vogue*, the designers studied together before establishing Nina Donis as an independent label, officially launching the project in 2000.[1]

Neretina and Pouppis have worked as a design partnership rather than dividing the label into individually credited creative roles. Their interviews describe the collections as the result of shared research and an ongoing exchange of visual references.[2]

## Early development

Soon after the label's launch, Nina Donis participated in international competitions and fashion festivals. At the **Festival International de Mode et de Photographie in Hyères** in 2001, the designers received a prize for their mixed men's and women's collection.[2][4]

The collection drew on Soviet visual culture and functional clothing. Contemporary reporting in *Le Monde* described the designers using a palette related to Soviet poster design and references to collective-farm workwear, while treating these sources primarily as visual and formal material.[4]

In 2003 Nina Donis was included in *Fashion Now*, the Taschen publication produced with *i-D* magazine that presented 150 designers selected by the magazine's editors.[5][6]

This recognition helped establish the label internationally before its participation in major European fashion-week schedules.

## London Fashion Week

Nina Donis appeared on the official London Fashion Week schedule in February 2005 with support from the British Fashion Council.[5]

*British Vogue* described the Moscow-based label before the show as an avant-garde addition to the London schedule and cited the designers' interest in finding new proportions, constructions, technologies and combinations within familiar forms of twentieth-century clothing.[5]

The Fall 2005 collection was subsequently reviewed by *Vogue*. The collection transformed elements of everyday urban clothing—including raincoats, tracksuits, down jackets and tailoring—through changes of proportion and construction.[7]

Sarah Mower described the designers' approach as rooted in observation of contemporary Moscow rather than stereotypical historical images of Russian dress. Pouppis explained that street layering during Moscow winters was one of the collection's points of departure.[7]

The label also presented work in Milan during its efforts to develop an international market.[2]

## Design language

Nina Donis is associated with a restrained form of experimental fashion in which familiar garments are altered through proportion, layering, colour and construction.

Recurring references in its collections have included:

- uniforms and workwear;
- sportswear and athletic clothing;
- Russian folk dress;
- Soviet architecture and graphic design;
- Constructivism and Suprematism;
- cinema, music and youth culture;
- functional clothing adapted to the Russian climate.[2][7]

Rather than reproducing these sources literally, Neretina and Pouppis have described them as part of a larger visual archive from which collections develop.[2]

Their work frequently combines simple silhouettes with unexpected colour relationships or altered garment functions. In the Fall 2005 collection, for example, conventional outerwear forms were transformed into dresses, skirts and hybrid garments, while sportswear shapes were reconstructed in tailoring fabrics.[7]

## Russian cultural references

Russian and Soviet culture have remained recurring sources for Nina Donis. In a 2015 interview with *1 Granary*, the designers identified literature, folk costume, Soviet architecture, posters, cinema, Yuri Gagarin, Russian rock of the 1980s and rave culture of the 1990s among the references that had entered their work.[2]

They also identified Russian and Soviet art as an important foundation of their aesthetic, while emphasizing that collections could begin with almost any visual stimulus, including contemporary popular culture and everyday objects.[2]

This approach distinguishes Nina Donis from fashion based primarily on historical reconstruction. References to Russian culture are mixed with international modernism, streetwear and contemporary visual culture.

## Independent fashion in Russia

Nina Donis developed largely as an independent operation rather than through the institutional structure of a large fashion company.

Neretina and Pouppis have spoken publicly about the difficulties of building an internationally distributed fashion business from Russia. They cited bureaucracy, legislation and the limited infrastructure available to independent designers as obstacles to expanding the company internationally despite interest from foreign buyers.[2]

Their experience became representative of a broader problem within Russian independent fashion: designers could receive international editorial attention and participate in European fashion weeks while still lacking the production, distribution and investment systems available in larger fashion markets.

The designers also described this absence of a rigid fashion system as a source of creative freedom, allowing them to work outside many conventional industry expectations.[2]

## Later work

Nina Donis continued producing collections through the 2010s. *Vogue* documented the label's Spring 2018 collection and described it as an established presence within Russian fashion.[1]

By this period the designers divided their time between Moscow and Cyprus while continuing to operate the label. In Moscow, Nina Donis was stocked by influential retailers including KM20 and Leform.[1]

The Spring 2018 coverage also demonstrated the continuity of the designers' approach: historical and cultural references were translated into simplified contemporary forms rather than reproduced directly. Sources cited for collections included Russian uniforms, traditional clothing and figures from international cultural history.[1]

## Recognition

Nina Donis has received several forms of international recognition:

| Year | Recognition or event |
| --- | --- |
| 2000 | Nina Donis officially launches as an independent label.[1][2] |
| 2001 | Receives a prize for a mixed collection at the Hyères fashion festival.[2][4] |
| 2003 | Included in *Fashion Now*, the Taschen/*i-D* selection of 150 important contemporary designers.[5][6] |
| 2005 | Presents a collection at London Fashion Week with British Fashion Council support.[5][7] |
| 2000s | Presents collections in London and Milan as part of attempts to enter the international market.[2] |
| 2017 | *Vogue* publishes the Nina Donis Spring 2018 collection and describes the label as an established presence in Russian fashion.[1] |

## Legacy

Nina Donis occupies an important position in the development of Russian independent fashion after the 1990s. The label emerged before the international interest in Russian and broader post-Soviet fashion that expanded substantially during the 2010s.

Its combination of uniforms, sportswear, modernist design, street observation and Russian cultural references anticipated several themes that later became prominent in international discussion of fashion from the region.

At the same time, Nina Donis maintained a distinct position from later streetwear-focused projects. Its collections have consistently emphasized garment construction, colour, proportion and the reinterpretation of established clothing types rather than branding or graphic identity alone.[2][7]

The original Indexmod entry already documented the label as founded by Neretina and Pouppis in 2000 and preserved an early collection chronology extending from the beginning of the 2000s.

Ognennaya Lady (Russian: Огненная Леди, “Fire Lady”) was the stage and fashion persona created by Russian artist, designer and performer Oleg Ognenny. Emerging from Moscow club culture in the early 1990s, the persona combined drag performance, fashion design, nightlife and theatrical spectacle and became associated with clubs including Ptuch and Shans.[1][2]

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## Origins

Oleg Ognenny has described creating the name **Ognennaya Lady** after performing in Moscow's early club scene with red hair and an almost entirely red visual image.[1]

In his recollections of 1990s Moscow nightlife, he described participating in a beauty contest at the club Mir and later appearing at Ptuch, Shans and other venues. Ognennaya Lady developed into a theatrical character rather than a conventional female impersonation act: performances could involve large casts and deliberately exaggerated costumes, gestures and imagery.[1]

Sources on the early Russian drag and club scene identify Ognennaya Lady as one of the recognizable Moscow club performers of the 1990s.[2][3]

## Ptuch and Moscow club culture

The persona was closely associated with the Moscow nightlife culture surrounding **Ptuch**, one of the influential clubs and magazines of the 1990s.

Ognenny recalled that Ognennaya Lady appeared on the cover of *Ptuch* together with the performer Artemida and staged large-scale performances in the club.[1] Contemporary retrospective accounts describe these events as hybrid productions combining costume, performance, music and club culture.

One remembered event turned fashion production itself into a performance: sewing machines were installed throughout the venue and participants competed to make an outfit for Ognennaya Lady.[1]

This overlap between nightlife, performance and clothing became a defining feature of the project.

## Fashion

Ognennaya Lady also functioned as a fashion-design identity.

Contemporary reporting from a Russian prêt-à-porter event documented a collection presented under the name **Ognennaya Lady**. Discussing the collection, the designer described childhood and a playful mood as its starting points and emphasized brightly coloured party clothing and the use of natural fabrics, particularly cotton.[4]

The surviving fashion press therefore supports treating Ognennaya Lady not only as a club persona but also as a fashion project associated with garments, collections and styling.

A 2001 fashion editorial cited in later academic research also credited customized and reconstructed clothing to **Ognennaya Lady**, placing the project within the period's interest in second-hand clothing, customization and alternative styling.[5]

## Performance and popular culture

Ognennaya Lady's activities extended beyond fashion shows. The character appeared within Moscow nightlife, performance events and popular entertainment.

Retrospective sources describe Ognennaya Lady as an important participant in the emergence of Russian club drag culture during the 1990s.[1][2] The persona was characterized by deliberate exaggeration and visual distortion rather than an attempt to construct a conventionally glamorous feminine image.

The character also appeared in Russian popular music culture. Sources on the history of Russian drag performance identify Ognennaya Lady with appearances around singer Nikita's late-1990s and early-2000s music projects.[2]

## Relationship to Oleg Ognenny

Ognennaya Lady was not a separate designer from Oleg Ognenny but a persona through which Ognenny worked in fashion, performance and club culture.

In later biographical descriptions the name **Oleg Ognenny** became the primary professional identity, while Ognennaya Lady was increasingly treated as the earlier stage and fashion persona.[1]

For this reason, the Indexmod entries should be read together:

- **Ognennaya Lady** — the historical persona, fashion identity and performance project;
- **Oleg Ognenny** — the artist and designer behind the persona and his later practice.

The earlier Indexmod chronology dated the Ognennaya Lady identity to 1993 and the transition to Oleg Ognenny to 2009. Available external sources clearly document the continuity between the two names, but do not provide enough reliable evidence to treat 2009 as a precise formal rebranding date. The transition is therefore better understood as gradual rather than as a documented corporate name change.

## Dsquared2 event at Arma

A surviving 2008 gallery from *Spletnik* identifies Ognennaya Lady among the guests at a Dsquared2 event held at the Moscow venue Arma. The photograph was credited to Aleksandr Kotin.[6]

This appearance is useful evidence that the Ognennaya Lady persona remained publicly recognizable in Moscow fashion and nightlife circles well after the 1990s.

## Design and performance identity

The significance of Ognennaya Lady lies partly in the absence of a strict division between designer, model, performer and artwork.

Clothing was used both as fashion and as a component of staged identity. Club performances could incorporate fashion-show structures, while fashion presentations retained elements of spectacle, parody and performance.

This places Ognennaya Lady within the wider experimental culture of post-Soviet Moscow, where fashion, nightlife, independent magazines, performance and contemporary art frequently overlapped.

Vincent Sung is a Korean-born Belgian photographer, visual artist and creative director associated with fashion, portraiture and editorial photography in Europe and Asia. Raised in Belgium and later active in Paris, Seoul and Bangkok, he became particularly associated with Korean fashion publishing in the late 1990s and 2000s and subsequently with photography, media production and independent cultural projects in Thailand.[1][2]

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## Background

Sung was born in Busan, South Korea, and was adopted by a Belgian family at the age of three. He grew up in Brussels, where he studied visual communication and photography and worked as an assistant to fashion photographers before moving to Paris in the early 1990s.[1][2]

He first returned to South Korea in 1995 and settled in Seoul in 1996. Contemporary profiles describe him as a Belgian-Korean photographer working between fashion, portraiture and commercial photography.[1][3]

## Fashion and editorial photography

After moving to Seoul, Sung worked with the Korean editions of international fashion and lifestyle magazines. KBS World identifies ELLE, Vogue, Harper's Bazaar and Marie Claire among the publications for which he worked, while a 2006 profile in the *Korea JoongAng Daily* described him as a freelancer whose photographs had appeared in magazines, newspapers and advertising.[1][3]

His practice combined studio fashion photography with portraiture and location-based editorial work. Sung has described his approach as using available environments and circumstances to construct a visual story rather than pursuing conventional prettiness as an end in itself.[3]

In addition to commercial assignments, Sung developed personal photographic projects. In 2010 KBS World discussed a solo fine-art photography exhibition that was described as his first such exhibition in eight years.[1] His later project *Intergalactic Encounters* was presented by LensCulture as part of his portfolio and used fashion photography to construct a science-fiction narrative around consumer culture.[4][5]

## Seoul, Bangkok and cultural projects

Sung's career has repeatedly crossed between photography and broader cultural production. After periods in Seoul and New York, he returned to Seoul and developed Visual Sponge Project, a content-production operation serving editorial and media clients.[2]

He relocated to Bangkok in 2010. His own professional biography records subsequent work in photography, creative direction, travel and lifestyle publishing, including roles connected with *Encounter Thailand* and the *Cool Bangkok* digital city guide.[2]

In 2014 Sung and Thomas Menard were associated with the creation of Soy Sauce Factory, an art and event space in a converted warehouse on Charoen Krung Road in Bangkok. Contemporary Bangkok press described the project as a multidisciplinary venue combining studio, exhibition, music and event functions.[2][6]

LensCulture continues to list Bangkok as Sung's location and presents both *Intergalactic Encounters* and an editorial fashion project made in Cambodia in his portfolio.[4]

## Practice

Sung's career sits at the intersection of fashion photography, editorial media and independent cultural production. His movement between Brussels, Paris, Seoul and Bangkok reflects a transnational professional trajectory in which European photographic training was applied to the rapidly expanding fashion-media industries of South Korea and, later, to creative and cultural projects in Southeast Asia.[1][2][3]

His published work includes fashion, celebrity and portrait photography as well as travel and lifestyle imagery. Alongside commissioned photography, he has worked as a creative director, producer and organizer of art-related projects.[1][2]

**Хоссейн Фармани** (англ. **Hossein Farmani**) — американо-иранский куратор, издатель, коллекционер фотографии и культурный предприниматель, основатель **Farmani Group**, **Lucie Awards** и ряда международных программ в области фотографии, дизайна и архитектуры. Его деятельность связана с издательскими проектами, фотографическими премиями, выставками, фестивалями и культурными институциями в США, Европе и Азии.[1][2][3]

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## Издательская и организационная деятельность

Farmani Group ведёт свою историю с **1985 года**, когда Фармани запустил в Лос-Анджелесе журнал **VUE**. Позднее группа развивала издательские, выставочные и конкурсные проекты в области фотографии, дизайна и архитектуры.[1]

К ранним инициативам Фармани относится **FotoFolio**, проект, посвящённый современной фотографии. В последующие десятилетия его деятельность расширилась от издательского дела к организации международных премий, выставок и культурных программ.[1]

## Lucie Awards и International Photography Awards

В **2003 году** были запущены **Lucie Awards** — международная программа признания достижений в фотографии. В том же году начала работу **Lucie Foundation**, связанная с премией и образовательными инициативами в области фотографии.[1][2]

Фармани является основателем и председателем Lucie Awards и основателем **International Photography Awards (IPA)**. IPA проводит ежегодный международный конкурс для профессиональных, любительских и студенческих фотографов.[2][3][4]

С Farmani Group также связаны **Prix de la Photographie Paris (PX3)**, **International Design Awards (IDA)**, **Moscow International Foto Awards (MIFA)**, **Tokyo International Foto Awards (TIFA)**, **Budapest International Foto Awards (BIFA)** и другие конкурсные программы.[1][2]

## Focus on AIDS

Фармани основал благотворительную инициативу **Focus on AIDS**, использовавшую фотографию и художественные мероприятия для сбора средств и привлечения внимания к проблеме ВИЧ/СПИДа. Lucie Foundation называет эту организацию одним из его ключевых общественных проектов.[2][3]

## Кураторская работа и коллекция

International Photography Awards сообщает, что Фармани курировал более **200 международных выставок**, читал лекции в университетах и участвовал в организации фотографических фестивалей в Северной Америке, Европе и Азии.[3]

Он также сформировал крупную частную коллекцию фотографии. Его работа как коллекционера, куратора и организатора связана с продвижением исторической и современной фотографии через выставки, конкурсы и образовательные программы.[3]

## House of Lucie и проекты в Азии

После переезда в Бангкок Фармани развивал в городе **Rooftop Gallery**, а в **2016 году** открыл там первое пространство **House of Lucie**, посвящённое фотографии и лауреатам Lucie Awards.[5][6]

В **2019 году** *The Art Newspaper* сообщала о создании Фармани двух фотографических центров в Кашане, Иран: **Karkhaneh Gallery** и **House of McCurry**. Параллельно он планировал открыть в городе музей **House of Lucie**, посвящённый фотографам — лауреатам Lucie Awards.[6]

Эти проекты были частью более широкой инициативы по расширению инфраструктуры фотографии за пределами традиционных западных культурных центров.[6]

## Farmani Group

Сегодня **Farmani Group** позиционирует себя как независимую международную организацию, объединяющую программы в области фотографии, дизайна и архитектуры. По данным самой группы, её сеть включает десятки конкурсов, премий, культурных инициатив и платформ, работающих более чем в ста странах.[1]

Среди направлений группы — фотография, графический и промышленный дизайн, архитектура, интерьер, световой дизайн и другие области визуальной культуры.[1][2]

**Art-o-rama** is an international contemporary-art fair in Marseille, France, founded in 2007 by Jérôme Pantalacci and Gaïd Beaulieu. Held at Friche la Belle de Mai, it concentrates on selected gallery projects and emerging artistic scenes, alongside contemporary editions and design. The fair is produced by Fræme in co-production with Friche la Belle de Mai. **[1][2][3]**

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## Origins

Art-o-rama developed from the professional milieu around Marseille gallerist Roger Pailhas. In 1996, Pailhas founded Art Dealers, inviting eight international galleries to exhibit inside his own gallery on the city's Old Port. After his death in 2005, Pantalacci and Beaulieu, who had worked with him, continued the idea of a small international fair rooted in Marseille. They established Art-o-rama in 2007. **[1]**

This history was revisited in 2025 through a tribute presentation organised by Gabrielle Bryers. Eight galleries shared an Art Dealers stand, including Air de Paris, Esther Schipper, Galleria Continua and Mennour. Each contributed a work, recalling the collaborative format of Pailhas's original initiative. **[1]**

## Organisation and format

The fair's organisers emphasise a selective, project-based format and the participation of emerging regional and international scenes. Its programme encompasses gallery presentations, art and design editions, screenings and conversations. An online component, the Salon Immatériel, extends the physical exhibition programme. **[2][3]**

The venue connects the commercial fair with a wider cultural programme. In 2026, the fair occupied spaces including La Cartonnerie, the Petit Plateau and the Grand Plateau; its ticket also gave access to accompanying exhibitions at the Friche. Screenings and conversations were offered free of charge. **[3]**

Art-o-rama also organises a regional itinerary introducing visitors to artistic institutions and sites across southern France, from Monaco to Montpellier, including Arles, Hyères, Nice and Marseille. This programme situates the fair within a wider regional network of galleries and cultural venues. **[2]**

## Twentieth edition

The twentieth edition took place from 28 to 30 August 2026. The venue's programme announced more than 60 galleries and publishers working in art and design, and approximately 100 artists, in addition to artists and designers associated with the Prix Région Sud. Pierre-Antoine Lalande selected the art participants for that prize programme, while Justinien Tribillon selected the design participants. **[3]**

**KALTBLUT Magazine** is an independent English-language fashion, art, photography, music and culture publication based in Berlin, Germany. Developed from the Berlin online magazine HONK! in the early 2010s, KALTBLUT combines fashion editorials, photography, interviews, emerging-artist features and cultural reporting, with a particular emphasis on independent creative scenes and new talent.[1][2][3]

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## History

KALTBLUT developed from **HONK! Magazine**, an online publication founded in Berlin in 2010. KALTBLUT's own archive preserves a transitional series of five issues published during 2011 under the name **KALTBLUT-HONK!**, followed by the first standalone KALTBLUT Collection, *Nude – Pur – Us*, released on 1 March 2012.[3][4]

The first standalone issue was a 400-page thematic edition devoted to nudity and included art, photography and fashion alongside contributors and subjects such as Gio Black Peter, Sam Sparro, Nir Arieli, Munroe Bergdorf and PETA. The publication described its early editorial idea as a "symbiosis" of art, photography, fashion and media and adopted English as its principal language in order to reach an international readership.[3]

KALTBLUT's current team page credits **Marcel Schlutt** and **Naikee Simoneau** as its founders. Schlutt is listed as editor-in-chief, fashion editor and art editor.[2]

In 2013, *Berliner Zeitung* included KALTBLUT in a report on Berlin's growing independent print-magazine culture. The newspaper described the publication as a large-format platform for young fashion, music and art and noted that it was being produced independently rather than through a conventional large publishing house.[5]

By 2014, KALTBLUT had developed both digital and physical editions. A profile in *Süddeutsche Zeitung* described the magazine as an international platform for lesser-known talent in fashion, art, music, film and photography and reported distribution through selected cultural and specialist outlets, including the Tate Modern in London and Centre Pompidou in Paris at that time.[6]

During the following years the magazine repeatedly adjusted its format. Marcel Schlutt stated in a 2019 interview that the earliest issues had resembled photographic books, while later editions became more focused on interviews. He also described print as important precisely because it gave the otherwise largely digital project a physical form.[7]

The issue archive documents **22 numbered KALTBLUT issues** through *The Class of 2025*, published in November 2024. That edition was presented as a celebration of thirteen years of the magazine and included fashion, art and music contributors including Tata Christiane, Effenberger Couture, Erin Wasson, EKKSTACY, Femme Bass Mafia and others.[4][8]

KALTBLUT has continued operating as an active online publication. In 2026 its editorial coverage included Berlin Fashion Week, independent fashion labels, emerging designers, queer and FLINTA* creative communities, photography, exhibitions, music and contemporary culture.[9]

## Editorial identity

KALTBLUT is structured around the overlap between several creative disciplines rather than around fashion alone. Its principal fields include:

- fashion and fashion photography;
- contemporary art and illustration;
- music;
- photography;
- film and moving image;
- interviews;
- Berlin cultural life;
- independent and emerging designers;
- queer and alternative creative cultures.[1][9]

The magazine's submission system also reflects this structure. Fashion, art, photography and illustration submissions are handled alongside music submissions, while fashion editorials are required to be conceived as complete stories rather than isolated images.[2]

A recurring feature of KALTBLUT has been the publication of work by emerging photographers, stylists, designers, models and artists alongside more established cultural figures. This approach was already identified by German press coverage in the early 2010s, which described the magazine as a platform intended to provide substantial space to people who had not yet entered mainstream fashion publishing.[5][6]

## Print and digital publishing

KALTBLUT began within the internet-based publishing culture of the early 2010s but has alternated between digital and print forms throughout its history. Its first standalone collection in 2012 was presented digitally as a large thematic publication, while subsequent editions were also made available as physical magazines.[3]

The print format became part of the publication's identity as an independent collectible object. At the same time, the website developed into a continuously updated editorial platform publishing fashion stories, interviews, premieres, art projects, event coverage and cultural reporting independently of the numbered magazine issues.[6][9]

This combination distinguishes KALTBLUT from a conventional fixed-period fashion magazine: the numbered issues function as curated thematic editions, while the website operates as an ongoing international cultural publication.

## Berlin context

Berlin is central to KALTBLUT's editorial and visual identity. The magazine emerged from the city's independent art, fashion, club and publishing environments and has regularly presented Berlin designers, photographers, musicians, exhibitions and events alongside international contributors.[5][7]

Its development belongs to a wider Berlin tradition of independent fashion and culture publishing in which magazines function not only as media outlets but also as creative platforms connecting photography, art direction, styling, music, nightlife and contemporary art.

## Chronology

| Year | Development |
| --- | --- |
| 2010 | HONK! Magazine, identified by KALTBLUT as its predecessor, is founded online in Berlin.[3] |
| 2011 | The archive records five transitional KALTBLUT-HONK! issues.[4] |

KALTBLUT occupies a position between an independent fashion magazine, a photography platform and a broader cultural publication. The publication also illustrates the development of independent fashion media during the internet era: beginning with online distribution, expanding into substantial print editions, and later maintaining both archival magazine issues and a continuously updated digital platform.

**Vanessa Pearce** is an Adelaide-based fashion designer and the founder and creative director of The Wolf Gang. Her label developed from accessories into an internationally stocked fashion and lifestyle business while retaining its design studio in South Australia. In 2026, she was a subject of ADL Fashion Week's *The Threads Between Us* campaign. **[1][2]**

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## The Wolf Gang

Pearce has described the label's beginnings as a response to objects and clothing she wanted but could not find in shops at home. Travel and encounters with other cultures informed the early work, which included accessories and artisan-made crochet. The business subsequently expanded into a broader lifestyle label. Its tenth anniversary was celebrated in April 2026. **[1]**

The brand's continued Adelaide base is part of Pearce's working approach. In a 2026 interview, she linked this decision to its slower pace of life and identified Revolve and Myer as stockists. **[1]**

## Design approach

Pearce's work emphasises colour, texture and distinctive pieces. Discussing garments such as the Abrigo coat and Luvia beaded mini dress, she described a design process centred on giving each item an identifiable character. Accessories and crochet remain points of continuity with the label's beginnings. **[1]**

For its announced tenth-anniversary runway, The Wolf Gang described a presentation built around statement prints, movement and texture, with Pearce responsible for styling and curation. **[3]**

## Adelaide retail and fashion events

The Wolf Gang participated in the inaugural ADL Fashion Week in October 2022 through a Rundle Mall pop-up. In the organiser's subsequent report, Pearce discussed how this physical presence allowed a largely online business to introduce its products and brand to local customers. The pop-up continued beyond the festival, and she reported increased South Australian website engagement following its opening. **[4]**

In 2026, Pearce joined the festival's *The Threads Between Us* campaign, alongside figures from fashion, broadcasting and hospitality, including Africola chef [Duncan Welgemoed](/duncan-welgemoed). The campaign situated individual style within the city's wider creative community. **[5]**

The Wolf Gang's first large-scale solo runway is scheduled for 10 October 2026 at Adelaide Town Hall as the closing show of ADL Fashion Week's official runway programme. Announced as a ten-year celebration, it is to be styled and curated by Pearce. As of this article's update, the show is forthcoming. **[2][3]**

***Updated 2026-09-07***

The **Islamic Arts Biennale** is an international biennial exhibition dedicated to the arts of Islamic civilizations, past and present. It is held in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, at the Western Hajj Terminal of King Abdulaziz International Airport, a landmark designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) and recipient of the Aga Khan Award for Architecture. The biennale was inaugurated in 2023 by the Diriyah Biennale Foundation and combines historical objects, religious artifacts, contemporary art, architecture, design, scholarship, and public programming. 

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## History

The first Islamic Arts Biennale took place from 23 January to 23 May 2023 under the title *Awwal Bait* (“First House”). The inaugural exhibition explored Islamic rituals and practices through historical objects and contemporary artistic perspectives. More than 600,000 visitors attended the first edition. 

The second edition, *And All That Is In Between*, was held from 25 January to 25 May 2025. It expanded the exhibition substantially, presenting more than 500 historical objects and contemporary artworks across five exhibition halls and outdoor spaces. More than 30 international institutions and more than 30 artists participated. 

The third edition is scheduled for 1 November 2027 to 1 March 2028 at the Western Hajj Terminal. The Diriyah Biennale Foundation has stated that the 2027 edition will expand collaboration with collecting institutions, artists, artisans, and scholars and further develop curatorial approaches to Islamic arts. 

| Year | Edition | Title / focus | Dates |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | First | *Awwal Bait* (“First House”) | 23 January – 23 May 2023 |
| 2025 | Second | *And All That Is In Between* | 25 January – 25 May 2025 |
| 2027–2028 | Third | Expanded exploration of Islamic arts | 1 November 2027 – 1 March 2028 |

## Venue

The biennale occupies the Western Hajj Terminal at King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah. Designed by SOM and completed in 1981, the terminal received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 1983. Its distinctive tensile-roof structures were designed to accommodate large numbers of pilgrims travelling to Makkah and Madinah. The reuse of the terminal as a cultural venue connects the exhibition to Jeddah's historical role as a gateway for Hajj and Umrah. 

The 2025 edition used approximately 100,000 square metres of exhibition and outdoor space. Its curatorial structure was divided into seven components: AlBidayah, AlMadar, AlMuqtani, AlMidhallah, AlMukarramah, AlMunawwarah, and AlMusalla. 

## Curatorial approach

The biennale places historical Islamic art in dialogue with contemporary artistic practice rather than presenting Islamic art solely as a historical category. The exhibitions bring together manuscripts, objects, religious artifacts, works of craftsmanship, architectural ideas, installations, sculpture, and newly commissioned contemporary works. 

The 2025 edition was directed by Julian Raby, Amin Jaffer, and Abdul Rahman Azzam, with Saudi artist Muhannad Shono serving as curator of contemporary art. Its theme, *And All That Is In Between*, examined the experience and expression of faith through feeling, thinking, and making. 

### AlMadar

AlMadar (“The Orbit”) brought together Islamic art objects from institutions in more than 21 countries. Its themes included celestial navigation, geography, mathematics, measurement, and the use of numerical systems to understand and represent the natural world. Historical objects were presented alongside contemporary commissions. 

Participating institutions in 2025 included the Louvre in Paris, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, the Museum of Islamic Art in Doha, the David Collection in Copenhagen, the Benaki Museum in Athens, the Ahmed Baba Institute in Timbuktu, the Qatar National Library, Ithra in Dhahran, the King Fahad National Library in Riyadh, and the Vatican Apostolic Library. 

### AlMuqtani

AlMuqtani (“Homage”) focused on the role of private collectors in preserving and interpreting Islamic visual and material culture. The 2025 presentation included works from the Al Thani Collection and the Furusiyyah Collection of Rifaat Sheikh El Ard, with particular emphasis on precious materials, jeweled objects, metalwork, and objects associated with chivalric traditions. 

### AlMidhallah

AlMidhallah (“The Canopy”) occupied outdoor areas of the biennale and explored the garden as a recurring element of Islamic civilization. New commissions considered relationships between nature, spirituality, environmental conditions, and contemporary social concerns. 

### Makkah and Madinah

Two permanent pavilions, AlMukarramah and AlMunawwarah, focus on Makkah and Madinah and their religious and cultural significance. The 2025 edition also presented objects associated with the holy cities, including the Kiswah, the cloth covering the Kaaba. The 2025 exhibition marked the first time the entire Kiswah was displayed outside Makkah. 

## Contemporary art

Contemporary art is a central component of the biennale. The 2025 edition commissioned new works by more than 30 artists from Saudi Arabia, the wider Arab world, and other regions. Participating artists included Ahmed Mater, Ala Younis, Imran Qureshi, Osman Yousefzada, Asif Khan, Takashi Kuribayashi, Charwei Tsai, Slavs and Tatars, and Muhannad Shono, among others. 

The commissions were conceived in dialogue with historical objects and the architecture of the Western Hajj Terminal. This approach positions contemporary art as part of an ongoing history of Islamic artistic and intellectual production rather than as a separate category. 

## AlMusalla Prize

The **AlMusalla Prize** is an international architectural competition associated with the Islamic Arts Biennale. It was established to explore contemporary forms of the *musalla*, a space for prayer and contemplation, with an emphasis on modularity, sustainability, adaptability, and the possibility of reuse beyond the biennale. 

For the 2025 edition, the prize was awarded to EAST Architecture Studio for *On Weaving*, developed with AKT II, artist Rayyane Tabet, and Sweco. The structure drew on regional weaving traditions and used materials derived from discarded date-palm fronds and fibres. Its modular design was intended to allow the structure to be dismantled and reassembled elsewhere. 

## Cultural significance

The Islamic Arts Biennale has established a recurring international platform in Saudi Arabia for the study and presentation of Islamic arts. Its location in Jeddah gives the exhibition a particular relationship to pilgrimage, while its institutional partnerships connect Saudi collections and cultural organizations with museums, libraries, and research institutions internationally. 

The biennale also forms part of the wider cultural programme developed by the Diriyah Biennale Foundation, which organizes both the Islamic Arts Biennale and the Diriyah Contemporary Art Biennale. The foundation describes these programmes as instruments for cultural exchange, artistic production, research, and the development of Saudi Arabia's contemporary cultural infrastructure.

***Updated 2026-09-03***

**Nigerian fashion** encompasses the textile traditions, forms of dress, designers, fashion houses, ateliers, retailers, media, streetwear communities and fashion events associated with Nigeria. Centred commercially and editorially on Lagos but drawing on textile and dress cultures from across the country, Nigerian fashion has become one of the most internationally visible fashion scenes in Africa. Its contemporary identity combines long-established practices such as àdìrẹ dyeing and aṣọ-òkè, akwete and okene weaving with tailoring, imported and locally produced printed cloth, luxury fashion, ready-to-wear, streetwear and experimental design.[1][2]

{{page:image}}

{{page:credit}}

## Textile traditions

There is no single traditional Nigerian fashion aesthetic. Nigeria contains numerous cultural and textile traditions whose materials, methods, forms and social meanings developed in different regions.

Among the most prominent is **àdìrẹ**, an indigo resist-dyed cloth historically produced by Yoruba women in south-western Nigeria. Cloth may be folded, stitched, tied or treated with cassava-starch resist before dyeing, producing distinctive patterns in indigo and white. The practice has changed repeatedly as makers adopted new cotton fabrics, tools and motifs. In contemporary fashion, àdìrẹ has been used by designers and labels including Maki Oh, Lagos Space Programme and Orange Culture.[1]

**Aṣọ-òkè** is a prestigious Yoruba strip-woven textile traditionally produced in narrow lengths that are subsequently joined together. Historically woven from materials including cotton and silk, it continues to appear in ceremonial dress while also being adapted by contemporary designers for jackets, dresses, trousers and other tailored garments.[1]

Other Nigerian textile traditions include **akwete**, associated with the Igbo weaving centre of Akwete in south-eastern Nigeria, and **okene**, a handwoven cloth associated with Ebira communities in central Nigeria. Mid-20th-century designer Shade Thomas-Fahm incorporated àdìrẹ, aṣọ-òkè, akwete and okene into modern garments, demonstrating how regional textile traditions could become materials for contemporary fashion rather than remaining fixed forms of historical dress.[2][7]

## Ankara and printed cloth

Brightly patterned **ankara** or African wax print is closely associated with Nigerian and wider West African dress, but its history is transnational rather than exclusively Nigerian or African. The cloth developed from European industrial attempts to reproduce Indonesian batik and became a major commodity in West African markets from the late 19th century. African consumers, traders and later manufacturers played an important role in determining its patterns, meanings and uses.[1]

Following independence, African textile companies increasingly participated in its production, while printed fabrics became closely connected with personal, regional and national identity. Nigerian designers subsequently transformed ankara through tailoring, embroidery, beading and combinations with other materials. Lisa Folawiyo, for example, built an internationally recognised design language around elaborately embellished printed textiles and contemporary silhouettes.[1][5]

## Independence and professional fashion design

Nigeria's independence in 1960 coincided with an important period in the professionalisation of fashion across newly independent African states. Fashion could operate simultaneously as commerce, modern urban culture and a means of expressing identities that were no longer defined primarily through European colonial institutions.[2]

**Shade Thomas-Fahm** is commonly described as Nigeria's first modern fashion designer. After studying at St Martin's School of Art in London, she returned to Lagos in 1960 and established **Maison Shade**. Her work combined Nigerian textiles and forms with ideas drawn from contemporary international fashion.[2]

Thomas-Fahm designed for an increasingly cosmopolitan urban clientele and modified established forms of Nigerian dress for modern everyday use. She created, among other innovations, a pre-tied gèlè headwrap and versions of the Yoruba ìró wrapper incorporating a zip. Her boutiques offered bespoke clothing as well as ready-to-wear lines, establishing a model in which Nigerian textile traditions could coexist with the structures of a modern fashion business.[2]

## Contemporary designers

During the 2000s and 2010s, a new generation of Nigerian designers developed brands that participated increasingly in international fashion while maintaining production, material or cultural relationships with Nigeria.

**Lisa Folawiyo** launched her label in 2005. Her work became particularly associated with transforming ankara through complex hand embellishment, tailoring and luxury construction.[5]

**Amaka Osakwe** founded **Maki Oh** in 2010. The label uses techniques including àdìrẹ while combining Nigerian cultural references with contemporary womenswear construction. Maki Oh's work has been important in demonstrating that traditional textile processes can function within conceptually driven contemporary fashion rather than simply as decorative markers of African identity.[6]

**Adebayo Oke-Lawal** founded **Orange Culture** in Lagos in 2011. The label became known for colour, fluid silhouettes and an approach to clothing that questions rigid distinctions between menswear and womenswear. Its work has also incorporated locally sourced fabrics and Nigerian craft traditions, including aṣọ-òkè.[8]

Other internationally visible Nigerian designers and labels include Kenneth Ize, Nkwo, Emmy Kasbit, Lagos Space Programme, IAMISIGO and several generations of Lagos-based independent fashion studios. Many work directly with weaving, dyeing and craft communities rather than treating traditional textiles only as historical references.[7]

## Lagos Fashion Week

A major institutional development was the establishment of **Lagos Fashion Week** in 2011 by Omoyemi Akerele through Style House Files. The platform was created to connect African designers with buyers, media, manufacturers, retailers and other parts of the fashion industry.[3][4]

Lagos Fashion Week developed beyond a conventional runway schedule into a year-round organisation supporting business development, education, sustainability and emerging designers. Its programmes have included Fashion Focus Africa, Green Access, Woven Threads and initiatives addressing manufacturing and the commercial development of African fashion.[3]

Its early editions included designers such as Lisa Folawiyo and Maki Oh, while later seasons presented Orange Culture, Kenneth Ize, IAMISIGO, Emmy Kasbit and numerous designers from Nigeria and elsewhere in Africa.[4]

By its fifteenth anniversary in 2025, Lagos Fashion Week had become one of the continent's most visible fashion platforms. Vogue reported more than 60 designers and approximately 15,000 visitors across the five-day 2025 edition.[4]

## Craft and contemporary luxury

A recurring characteristic of contemporary Nigerian fashion is the use of traditional textile production within forms normally associated with international luxury and designer fashion.

Kenneth Ize has worked extensively with aṣọ-òkè and developed production relationships with Nigerian weaving communities. Nkwo Onwuka created **Dakala cloth**, a textile made from discarded denim, end-of-line materials and cutting-room waste. Emmy Kasbit has used akwete weaving within contemporary collections.[7]

These practices have contributed to a broader reassessment of craft. Rather than separating craft from fashion, many Nigerian designers treat weaving, dyeing, embroidery and hand-finishing as sources of technical innovation and as part of the economic structure of their labels.[7]

## Streetwear and youth culture

Nigerian fashion also includes an expanding streetwear scene shaped by music, nightlife, skate culture, photography, social media and Lagos youth culture.

The **Street Souk** convention, founded in Lagos by Ireti Zaccheaus in 2018, became an important meeting point for independent streetwear brands and young consumers. The V&A has identified Lagos, alongside Cape Town, as one of the principal centres of a new generation of African streetwear in which global references to hip-hop and skateboarding are recombined with local graphics, language and cultural references.[8]

Streetwear has broadened the idea of the Nigerian fashion industry beyond formal designer labels and couture, creating a scene in which small brands, photographers, musicians, stylists and digital creators often operate within the same creative networks.

## Fashion media

The expansion of Nigerian digital media has been important to the visibility of the fashion scene. Publications and online platforms document runway collections, designers, beauty, celebrity style and fashion-business developments for audiences inside and outside Nigeria.

**BellaNaija Style**, launched as a dedicated fashion and lifestyle publication in 2017 within the BellaNaija media network, has become one of the platforms documenting Nigerian and African designers, fashion weeks, street style and the wider creative industries.[10]

Digital publishing and social media have helped Nigerian designers circulate images and collections internationally without depending entirely on established European or American fashion publications.

## International visibility

Nigerian designers have increasingly appeared within international retail, museums and fashion-week systems. Lisa Folawiyo's work has been stocked internationally; Maki Oh gained international recognition for its contemporary use of Nigerian textile traditions; Kenneth Ize has presented in Paris; and Orange Culture has presented collections outside Nigeria while maintaining strong connections with Lagos-based production and collaborators.[4][7][8]

The Victoria and Albert Museum's **Africa Fashion** exhibition, held in London from 2022 to 2023, placed Nigerian designers within a broader history of post-independence and contemporary African fashion. Shade Thomas-Fahm appeared among the pioneering mid-20th-century figures, while contemporary Nigerian work represented the continuing transformation of textile, craft and fashion practice.[9]

The internationalisation of Nigerian fashion has therefore not meant the replacement of local references by a single global aesthetic. Much of its most influential work instead depends on exchanges between Lagos and other fashion centres, between hand production and industrial systems, and between inherited forms of dress and new approaches to gender, sustainability, luxury and street culture.

| Late 19th century | Ankara and related printed cottons develop a major consumer market in West Africa.[1] |
| Early 20th century | Àdìrẹ production expands commercially in south-western Nigeria, particularly through centres such as Abeokuta and Ibadan.[1] |
| 1960 | Nigeria gains independence; Shade Thomas-Fahm returns to Lagos and establishes Maison Shade.[2] |
| 2005 | Lisa Folawiyo launches her fashion label.[5] |
| 2010 | Amaka Osakwe establishes Maki Oh.[6] |
| 2011 | Lagos Fashion Week is founded; Adebayo Oke-Lawal launches Orange Culture.[3][4] |
| 2018 | Ireti Zaccheaus establishes Street Souk in Lagos, contributing to the organisation of the city's emerging streetwear community.[8] |
| 2020 | Kenneth Ize presents at Paris Fashion Week, bringing contemporary Nigerian aṣọ-òkè-based design to an expanded international audience.[7] |

| 2025 | Lagos Fashion Week celebrates its fifteenth anniversary with more than 60 designers on the programme.[4] |
| 2026 | Nigerian fashion continues to operate across craft, luxury, streetwear, media and international fashion-week networks.[1][3][7] |
